tasks.title: Specify worlds as a hosted platform: connect, join, scenarios, runs, clean data, RL environments
tasks.why: Aaron: this is a core, foundational part and must be specified well before breadth. Heavy infrastructure on every sandbox makes no sense; it must be easy to create a simulation, bring a hundred or two hundred testers and agents through scenarios, and get clean training data and environments for reinforcement learning. Today the pieces are scattered across five documents and a few dozen records.
evidence: lane/worlds-spec merged (141885c, 54e1af1): docs/design/worlds-platform.md, 38 operations, the Worlds page

tasks.title: Close the gap between the checks and the book's tests
tasks.why: The first real score is 8 of 4,724. The test sites' checks are real, but 56 of them prove something the book has no test for, 39 prove only part of one, and 143 of the 146 tests of the thin-line journeys have no check at all.

tasks.title: Core: sign-in and signing for people
tasks.why: Aaron: this belongs to Capxul Core and is on the critical path, though not yet. Agents hold keys and sign with them. People need a way to prove who they are and to approve a transaction, and no person should use a world's screens before it exists.

tasks.title: The loop: make it trustworthy enough to run tasks unattended
tasks.why: The first version works but is not yet safe to leave alone: its budget is counted in turns and time, not money; its rules on what an agent may run are a filter, not a sandbox; steering a running agent and the heavy sandbox are untested; and it is 1,200 lines against a cap of 800.

tasks.title: Worlds 1: the lean service, a registry of worlds, and twenty measured
tasks.why: Everything else in the platform stands on a world being cheap. The figure of 0.15 GiB for a world's Capxul part is an estimate until it is measured.

tasks.title: Worlds 2: a first hosted core world, and joining it with a key
tasks.why: Aaron: if they have already got keys, here is a new environment. This is the smallest version of that.

tasks.title: Worlds 3: templates, the seed adapter and the first scenario
tasks.why: A world is only useful with companies and events in it. The old scenario companies are the source.

tasks.title: Worlds 4: cohorts, runs and the accepted dataset
tasks.why: The product of a run is clean data. A hundred or two hundred testers and agents need runs that are scheduled, watched, closed and checked.

tasks.title: Worlds 5: a core world as a learning environment
tasks.why: Aaron: as we move into reinforcement learning we need environments and clean data.

tasks.title: Tidy the repository so a person can find their way
tasks.why: Aaron opened the repository and could not make sense of it: run folders at the top level, twenty loose scripts and thirty-one old workflow scripts in tools, a spike still sitting there, books beside a book package, and a loop package he could not follow.

tasks.title: Rename the book to the blueprint
tasks.why: Aaron: call it blueprint, because nothing else sounds like it. The word book does not say what the thing is, and books/ beside packages/book confused him.

tasks.title: A Live page: what is running, on what, and whether it is moving
tasks.why: Aaron asked to see the agents that are running: what each is working on, when it last did anything, how many tool calls. He had also said he felt lost about what is in flight.

path.why: Worlds as a hosted platform is now specified. The loop runner is made trustworthy next, so later tasks run through it. Then the checks are lined up with the book's tests so the score is real, time is proved on the scoreboard, the AWS side is written in, and telemetry is the remaining bulk. The old decisions and the entry documents are cleaned up before Aaron is asked to accept the book. Beside this path, the cloud milestone builds the platform: the lean service, a first hosted world, joining, scenarios, runs and the dataset.

notes.text: The book is cut to the new shape and the plugs, sites, worlds and the door are written in, much of it still marked as assumption. The real contracts run in the repository. The spike that proves the door and the clock is running. Three things wait on Aaron: equity, the payroll route, and the AWS sign-in for the machine.
Done now also means a shared world running a thin line through the whole stack on the machine. That needs Aaron's AWS sign-in, the subdomain and the DNS records before it can start.

The plan page is live and is now where the work is tracked. Four things wait on Aaron: the AWS sign-in with the subdomain and DNS records, the cost audit's switch-offs, equity, and the payroll filing route. The door and clock spike and the contracts' deeper tests are still running.

The plan now explains itself: an outline, and a page for every milestone and task. Everything that waits on Aaron is in one list on the Questions page, and his answers are saved to plan/answers.jsonl on this Mac. The door, the recorder, the clock and snapshots are built on the test sites; the coordinator is re-running their checks before closing that task.

Aaron answered every question. Six are accepted. Seasons are dropped for now. Payroll targets the United States first. The clock question is open again: he wants to understand what can go wrong, and a study is being written.

10 November 2026 (coordinator): the clock is settled: Aaron accepted the recommendation, option A of the time study, and the book records it with six tests (m1-time-proof, first on the path). The spikes' evidence is in the book. The jurisdiction is open again: Aaron left it open, preferring a crypto-friendly place (the UAE a candidate), so payroll waits on a comparison of places (m1-payroll-uk).

Aaron has handed over: the coordinator runs the climb. His answers are applied, the clock is settled for option A and proved on the test sites, the jurisdiction is open, and the contract records match the code with a check. Before the bulk work starts, two things change: every thread gets its own working copy, and a scoreboard runs the book's tests so that done is a result, not a report. One thing waits on Aaron: the four DNS records for worlds.capxul.com.

Handoff note, 10 November, midday. Aaron is away and has handed over. Done and merged: the book cut and reshaped (201 operations, 0 problems), his answers applied, the clock settled for option A and proved on the test sites (119 of 119, the coordinator's own run), the contract records matching the code with a check, an example on every operation, the plan page and the one inbox with saved answers, the worlds machine in AWS with its DNS zone and the four NS records at Namecheap. Running in their own lanes: the scoreboard (lane/scoreboard), the loop runner on pi-durable in its own package (lane/loop), the certificate (machine thread). Next: merge those when their checks pass, prove time on the scoreboard, the AWS side as records, telemetry on every operation, the lean service, the hosted bench image, the first shared world. Nothing waits on Aaron right now. The jurisdiction is open; equity, the hosted FDE and individuals are parked.

Aaron asked for worlds as a hosted platform to be specified well, before breadth: easy to create a simulation, to bring a hundred or two hundred testers and agents through scenarios, and to get clean data and environments for learning. It was scattered across documents. It is now one task, first on the path, being written into the book with its own page on the portal.

Worlds as a hosted platform is specified: one design in the book and on the portal's Worlds page, with 38 commands for scenarios, runs, cohorts, joining, datasets and the learning interface. Building it is five tasks in the cloud milestone, starting with the lean service. The loop runner is merged; its real run was blocked by model errors from the gateway, which is being looked at.

Handoff note, 10 November, afternoon. Merged today: the cut and reshaped blueprint (still called the book in the code; a rename to blueprint is a task), Aaron's answers, an example on every operation, the contract check, the scoreboard (first score 8 of 4,724), the loop runner on pi-durable in packages/loop, and worlds as a hosted platform with its Worlds page. The worlds machine, its DNS and its certificate exist in AWS. In flight: lining the checks up with the blueprint's tests (lane/eval-coverage), a Live page for running agents (lane/live-page), and the repository tidy-up as its own session (repo-tidy), with the rename to blueprint in its second stage. Next on the path: make the loop trustworthy (its real run was blocked by model errors from the gateway), prove time on the scoreboard, the AWS side as records, telemetry. Aaron's standing decisions: keep LiteLLM; people's sign-in is a later Core design; agents first; the first jurisdiction is open; he no longer wants cost reports relayed. The portal is at localhost:4391 and, over Tailscale, at macbook.tail4b9a40.ts.net:8443.
